headline: Gilt yields near 19-year high as markets bet on a Bank of England rate rise

terms.meaning: The interest rate the government pays to borrow by selling gilts, which are UK government bonds.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which affects mortgages, loans and savings.
Leaning towards higher interest rates to bring prices under control.

levels.headline: Gilt yields near 19-year high as markets bet on a Bank of England rate rise
levels.body:
The UK government's cost of borrowing is close to its highest level in nearly two decades, and investors now expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month. The 10-year gilt yield reached 5.51% on 8 October, the highest since July 2007, and was still around 5.44% at Monday's close. The 30-year yield has been above 6%, a level not seen since 1998.
Money markets price about a 90% chance that the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will lift Bank Rate by a quarter of a point, from 3.75% to 4.0%, on 5 November. Governor Andrew Bailey said at the September meeting that the longer energy-driven volatility lasts, the more likely a rise becomes.
Economists are less certain. In a Reuters poll only about one in eight expected a November move, although Oxford Economics forecasts rises in November and February, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%. The Budget on 28 October adds to the pressure on the public finances.
levels.why: It shows how the energy shock is feeding into borrowing costs for the government, businesses and homeowners.

levels.headline: Gilt yields stay near 19-year highs as a Bank Rate rise looks likely
levels.body:
Government borrowing costs remain close to their highest in almost two decades, and markets expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates on 5 November. The 10-year gilt yield peaked at 5.51% on 8 October, its highest since July 2007, and was about 5.44% on Monday. Yields on 30-year gilts have topped 6%, last seen in 1998.
Traders put the chance of a quarter-point rise in Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4.0%, at roughly 90%. Governor Andrew Bailey told the September meeting that continued volatility in energy prices makes a rise more likely.
Forecasters disagree. A Reuters poll found only around one in eight economists expecting a move in November, while Oxford Economics expects increases in both November and February, which would take Bank Rate to 4.25%. Any rise would affect mortgage and loan costs, and the Chancellor's Budget on 28 October is due soon after.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs for government and households could shape both the Budget and family finances.

levels.headline: Borrowing costs for the UK government near their highest since 2007
levels.body:
The interest rate the government pays to borrow is close to a 19-year high, and investors expect the Bank of England to raise its own rate next month. The yield on 10-year gilts, which are UK government bonds, reached 5.51% on 8 October. That is the highest since July 2007. The 30-year yield has been above 6%, a level last seen in 1998.
Financial markets believe there is about a 90% chance that the Bank will raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4.0% on 5 November. Governor Andrew Bailey has said the longer energy price swings continue, the more likely a rise becomes.
Not everyone agrees. In a Reuters poll only about one in eight economists expected a rise in November, but Oxford Economics thinks the Bank will raise rates in November and again in February, to 4.25%. Chancellor John Healey delivers his Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: Rising rates make borrowing dearer for the government, businesses and anyone with a loan or mortgage.

levels.headline: Government borrowing costs hit a 19-year high as rate rise looms
levels.body:
The UK government is paying more to borrow than at any time since 2007, and the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates next month. On 8 October the yield on 10-year gilts, the bonds the government sells to raise money, hit 5.51%. For 30-year gilts the yield has passed 6%, last seen in 1998.
Markets think there is a 90% chance that the Bank will raise its main rate, Bank Rate, by a quarter of a point to 4.0% on 5 November. It is now 3.75%. Governor Andrew Bailey said that the longer the unsteady energy prices last, the more likely a rise will be needed.
Some experts are not so sure. A Reuters poll found only one in eight economists expected a November rise. Oxford Economics expects rises in November and February. The Chancellor will set out his Budget on 28 October, with less room for spending than hoped.
levels.why: A rate rise would make mortgages and loans dearer and leave the Chancellor with less room in the Budget.

levels.headline: The government is paying more to borrow, and interest rates may follow
levels.body:
It now costs the UK government more to borrow than it has for 19 years. The government raises money by selling gilts, which are bonds, and the interest it pays on them is called the yield. The 10-year yield hit 5.51% on 8 October, the highest since 2007, and 30-year yields have passed 6%.
This is important because the Bank of England sets Bank Rate, its main interest rate, which is 3.75% today. Traders believe there is a 90% chance that the Bank raises it to 4.0% on 5 November. Governor Andrew Bailey has said that if energy prices stay jumpy, a rise becomes more likely.
Not every expert agrees. One survey found that only about one in eight economists expected a rise in November. A higher Bank Rate usually makes mortgages and loans dearer, and the Chancellor delivers his Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make loans and mortgages cost more and squeeze the government's budget.

levels.headline: What a 19-year high in government borrowing costs means
levels.body:
It now costs the UK government more to borrow money than it has for 19 years. The government borrows by selling bonds called gilts. The yield is the interest rate on them. The 10-year gilt yield reached 5.51% on 8 October, the highest since 2007, and the 30-year yield has gone above 6%.
This matters because the Bank of England may raise its main interest rate, called Bank Rate, on 5 November. It is 3.75% now. Markets think there is about a 90% chance it goes up by a quarter of a point to 4.0%. The Bank's Governor, Andrew Bailey, has said that if energy prices keep jumping around, a rise is more likely.
Economists are split. One survey found only about one in eight expected a rise in November. Banks use Bank Rate to set the price of mortgages and loans, so a rise could cost families more. The Budget is on 28 October.
levels.why: Higher interest rates can raise the cost of mortgages and loans for ordinary families.

levels.headline: Borrowing is getting more expensive, and interest rates may go up
levels.body:
The government has to pay more to borrow money than it has for almost twenty years. It borrows by selling bonds called gilts, and the rate it pays on them is called the yield. On 8 October the yield on a 10-year gilt reached 5.51%. That is the highest since 2007.
The Bank of England may also raise its main interest rate on 5 November. This rate is called Bank Rate and it is 3.75% today. Traders think there is about a 90% chance it will go up to 4.0%. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, says a rise is more likely if energy prices keep swinging up and down.
Not all experts agree. A survey found only about one in eight thought it would rise in November. If rates do rise, mortgages and loans can cost more each month. The government will also have less money to spend when it sets out its Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: If interest rates rise, loans and mortgages can cost families more.

levels.headline: Why borrowing costs have gone up and what could happen next
levels.body:
When the government needs money, it sells bonds called gilts. It promises to pay people back with interest. That interest rate is called the yield, and right now it is very high. It is the highest for 19 years. This is because energy prices have jumped, and that makes prices rise in the shops too.
The Bank of England wants prices to stay steady. One tool it uses is a rate called Bank Rate, which is 3.75%. Banks use it to set what they charge for mortgages and loans. Traders think the Bank will raise it to 4.0% on 5 November. The chance is about nine in ten.
Some experts think the Bank will wait. Only about one in eight said they expected a rise in November in one survey. A higher rate would make loans cost more. It would also mean the government has less money to spend when it announces its Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: A higher interest rate means that borrowing money costs more, for families and for the government.

levels.headline: Interest rates might go up, and that could cost families more
levels.body:
Imagine the government borrows money like you might borrow from a friend. It has to pay a bit extra back. That extra is called interest. Right now, the government has to pay more extra than it has for 19 years.
There is another interest rate too. The Bank of England sets it. People call it Bank Rate and it is 3.75% now. Banks use it to decide what to charge for loans and for mortgages, which are loans for buying a house. Many people think the Bank will make it a little bigger, to 4.0%, on 5 November.
Why? Energy prices have gone up a lot because of a war. That makes many things in shops cost more. Raising the rate is one way to slow prices down. But some experts are not sure it will happen. If it does, families with loans may pay a bit more each month.
levels.why: Higher rates can mean families pay more each month on loans.

levels.headline: Why money is getting more expensive to borrow
levels.body:
Think about the school tuck shop. Say you borrow some pocket money and promise to give it back with a little extra. That extra is called interest. When lots of people want extra, the extra gets bigger.
The government borrows money too. Right now it has to pay back more extra than for many years. A group called the Bank of England also has a special rate that sets how expensive borrowing is for grown-ups. Today it is 3.75%. Lots of people think the Bank will make it a little bigger on 5 November. They think it could go to 4.0%.
Why? Things in shops have been getting dearer because fuel costs more. Making borrowing dearer can help slow that down. But it can also mean that families who owe money pay a bit more each month. Some experts think the Bank might wait and not change it yet.
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, families with loans may have less to spend.

headline: Chancellor Healey's Budget on 28 October comes with a halved fiscal buffer

terms.meaning: The gap between what the government plans to borrow and the limit it has set itself.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the public finances.
Keeping tax bands at the same level, so more pay falls into higher bands as wages rise.

levels.headline: Chancellor Healey's Budget on 28 October comes with a halved fiscal buffer
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026, two weeks from today. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the independent forecaster, will publish its updated economic and fiscal forecast on the same day. Mr Healey took the job under Prime Minister Andy Burnham on 20 July.
PwC estimates that movements in bond yields and interest rates have roughly halved the Chancellor's fiscal headroom, the buffer between his plans and his own borrowing rules, to about £14 billion. Higher yields raise the cost of government borrowing and eat into that buffer, as this week's gilt market moves show.
The government has repeated its pledge not to raise income tax rates, and income tax thresholds are already frozen until April 2031. Commentators therefore expect attention to fall on other taxes, such as capital gains tax, while corporation tax for large companies is expected to stay at 25%.
levels.why: The size of the buffer limits what the government can spend, cut or tax in the Budget.

levels.headline: Two weeks to the Budget, and the Chancellor has little room to manoeuvre
levels.body:
The Autumn Budget is on Wednesday 28 October, and Chancellor John Healey has less room than he expected. He took the job under Prime Minister Andy Burnham on 20 July. The OBR, the official forecaster, will publish new forecasts on the same day.
PwC estimates that higher bond yields and interest rates have roughly halved his fiscal headroom, the cushion between his plans and his borrowing rules, to around £14 billion. When yields rise, the government pays more to borrow, which uses up the cushion.
Ministers have repeated their pledge not to raise income tax rates, and thresholds stay frozen until April 2031. Analysts therefore point to capital gains tax as a possible target, while corporation tax for large firms is expected to stay at 25%. With gilt yields near 19-year highs, the numbers the OBR publishes will be watched closely.
levels.why: It shows how borrowing costs limit what any Chancellor can promise.

levels.headline: Budget due on 28 October as the Chancellor's safety margin shrinks
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will present his Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The OBR, the independent body that checks the government's sums, will publish its forecasts at the same time. Mr Healey has been Chancellor since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July.
According to PwC, rising bond yields and interest rates have cut his headroom roughly in half, to about £14 billion. Headroom is the gap between the government's plans and the borrowing rules it has set itself. When it costs more to borrow, that gap gets smaller.
The government says it will not raise income tax rates, and the tax bands stay frozen until April 2031. Commentators therefore think other taxes, such as capital gains tax, could be looked at. Corporation tax for large companies is expected to stay at 25%. Mayors may also be given a bigger share of locally raised money.
levels.why: The Budget decides how much tax people pay and how much the government spends.

levels.headline: The Budget is two weeks away and the Chancellor has less money to play with
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will deliver the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. This is when the government sets out its plans for taxes and spending. On the same day, the OBR, an independent group that forecasts the economy, will publish its own predictions. Mr Healey became Chancellor on 20 July when Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.
The firm PwC says his safety margin has roughly halved, to about £14 billion. This margin is called headroom. It is the gap between what the government plans to borrow and the limit it has set. Higher borrowing costs have shrunk it.
Ministers have said they will not raise income tax rates, and the tax bands are frozen until April 2031. So people expect changes to other taxes, such as capital gains tax. Tax for big companies is expected to stay at 25%.
levels.why: It affects the taxes we pay and the money available for public services.

levels.headline: The Budget is on 28 October, and the Chancellor has less spare money
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will deliver the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. This is the day when the government explains how it will raise money through taxes and how it will spend it. An independent forecaster, the OBR, will publish its predictions for the economy on the same day.
The government has a borrowing rule, and the gap between its plans and that limit is called headroom. The firm PwC estimates it has roughly halved, to about £14 billion, because borrowing now costs more.
Ministers have promised not to raise the rate of income tax, and tax bands stay frozen until April 2031. So commentators think other taxes, such as capital gains tax, could change instead. Tax for large companies is expected to stay at 25%.
levels.why: The Budget decides how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: What the Chancellor's Budget is, and why money is tight this year
levels.body:
Once a year the Chancellor tells the country how the government will raise money and how it will spend it. This is called the Budget. This year it is on Wednesday 28 October. The Chancellor is John Healey. An independent group, the OBR, will share its own guess about how the economy will do on the same day.
The government has a rule about how much it can borrow. The space between its plans and that limit is called headroom. The firm PwC says headroom has roughly halved to about £14 billion. That happened because it now costs more to borrow money.
Ministers have promised not to raise income tax rates, and tax bands stay frozen until April 2031. So people think other taxes may change, like the tax on profits from selling things that have grown in value. Tax for big firms is expected to stay at 25%.
levels.why: The Budget affects how much tax we pay and how much money public services get.

levels.headline: The Budget is coming, and there is less spare money than before
levels.body:
Every year the Chancellor makes a big speech called the Budget. It says what taxes will be and how the government will spend money. This year the speech is on Wednesday 28 October. The Chancellor is John Healey.
The government has a rule about how much money it can borrow. The room it has left under that rule is called headroom. A company called PwC says the headroom has gone down by about half, to around £14 billion. It is smaller because borrowing has become more expensive.
The government has promised it will not put up the rate of income tax. Tax bands are also frozen until April 2031. So experts guess that other taxes might change instead. Big companies are expected to keep paying 25% tax on their profits. An independent group called the OBR will share its forecasts on the same day.
levels.why: The Budget changes how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: What is the Budget and why does the government have less money?
levels.body:
The government is a bit like a big family with a budget. Once a year, the person in charge of the money, called the Chancellor, explains the plan. This year that is John Healey, and he will do it on Wednesday 28 October.
The government also has a rule about how much it can borrow. The extra space under the rule is called headroom. This space has become about half as big, to roughly £14 billion. That is because borrowing money now costs more than it used to.
The government has promised not to raise income tax. That is the tax taken from people's wages. The levels at which people start paying more tax will stay the same until 2031. So experts think other taxes might change instead. Another group, the OBR, will share its forecast about the economy on the same day.
levels.why: It decides what the government can pay for, like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The government has less spare money, and a big plan is coming
levels.body:
Imagine your family has a weekly spending plan. Each year the person who looks after the government's money, called the Chancellor, shares the plan. This year he is called John Healey. He will do it on 28 October.
But the government has less spare money than it hoped. Borrowing money costs more now, like a loan that asks for more back. The spare space has become about half as big. It is now about £14 billion, which is still a very large number.
The government has promised it will not make the main tax on wages bigger. Some experts guess that other taxes may change instead. A group of number experts called the OBR will tell everyone what they think will happen to the economy on the same day.
levels.why: The plan decides how much money is left for things like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: A big money plan is coming for the whole country
levels.body:
Think of the school having a plan for how to spend its money. The country has a plan like that too. It is called the Budget. A person called the Chancellor tells everybody what it is. The Chancellor is called John Healey. He will say it on 28 October.
The country has less spare money than it hoped. It is a bit like a family whose rent went up. The spare money has become about half as big. It is still around £14 billion. That is a very big number.
The country has promised that it will not ask people to pay more on the money they earn at work. But some grown-ups think other things might cost more instead. Some number experts, called the OBR, will tell everybody what they think will happen to the money in the country.
levels.why: It decides how the country spends its money on things like schools.

headline: Energy price cap rises 4% but VAT is scrapped on electricity

terms.meaning: Ofgem's limit on the price per unit that suppliers can charge for gas and electricity, set every three months.
Value Added Tax, a sales tax added to many goods and services.
The price energy firms pay for gas before it is sold to homes.

levels.headline: Energy price cap rises 4% but VAT is scrapped on electricity
levels.body:
Ofgem's energy price cap rose by 4% on 1 October to £1,723 a year for a typical household, which the regulator says reflects higher wholesale gas prices. The cap covers the period from 1 October to 31 December 2026. It limits the price per unit of energy and does not limit the total bill, so households that use more still pay more.
On the same day, VAT on household electricity fell from 5% to 0%. The cut runs only until 31 March 2027, and gas keeps its 5% rate. Estimates put the typical saving at about £45 a year, and Ofgem says electricity bills will stay broadly stable as a result.
Consumer expert Martin Lewis has argued that the rising cap will absorb much of the saving. Some sources quote a different size for the rise, such as 3.6%, because of how the VAT change is counted.
levels.why: It shows how far the government's tax cut offsets higher gas prices in household bills.

levels.headline: Price cap up 4% as VAT comes off household electricity
levels.body:
Ofgem's price cap went up by 4% on 1 October, to £1,723 a year for a typical household. The regulator says higher wholesale gas prices are the cause. The cap applies until 31 December 2026 and limits the price per unit, not the total bill.
At the same time, VAT on domestic electricity fell from 5% to nothing. That cut lasts until 31 March 2027, while gas stays at 5%. The typical saving is estimated at around £45 a year, and Ofgem says this keeps electricity bills broadly stable.
Martin Lewis of MoneySavingExpert has said the higher cap will swallow much of the benefit. Reported figures for the rise vary slightly, with some outlets giving 3.6%, depending on whether the VAT change is included. The Budget on 28 October may bring further help or further pressure.
levels.why: It affects what millions of households pay to heat and light their homes this winter.

levels.headline: Energy bills: price cap rises 4% but electricity VAT is cut to zero
levels.body:
The energy price cap rose by 4% on 1 October, to £1,723 a year for a typical household, according to Ofgem, the energy regulator. It says higher wholesale gas prices pushed the cap up. The new cap lasts until 31 December.
The government has also cut VAT on household electricity from 5% to 0% from 1 October until 31 March 2027. Gas still carries VAT at 5%. A typical home might save about £45 a year, and Ofgem says electricity bills will stay broadly stable.
However, Martin Lewis of MoneySavingExpert says the higher cap will take back much of that saving. The cap limits the price paid for each unit of energy, so a household that uses more energy will still pay more in total. Some reports give the rise as 3.6% rather than 4%.
levels.why: It shows whether tax cuts can offset higher energy prices for ordinary households.

levels.headline: Energy bills go up 4%, but there is no VAT on electricity now
levels.body:
Since 1 October, the energy price cap has been £1,723 a year for a typical home. That is 4% more than before. Ofgem, the regulator that sets the cap, says gas costs more on the wholesale market, which is where energy companies buy it. The cap lasts until 31 December.
The cap limits the price for each unit of energy, not the whole bill. If you use more, you pay more.
Also from 1 October, VAT on household electricity has gone from 5% to nothing. VAT is a tax added to many things we buy. This lasts until 31 March 2027, and gas still has 5% VAT. A typical household might save around £45 a year. The money expert Martin Lewis says the higher cap will cancel out much of this. Some reports give a slightly different figure for the rise.
levels.why: It shows how tax changes and energy prices together decide what we pay at home.

levels.headline: Energy bills: the price cap is up 4%, but VAT is off electricity
levels.body:
On 1 October, Ofgem's energy price cap rose by 4%, to £1,723 a year for a typical household. Ofgem is the energy regulator, and it says gas has become more expensive to buy. The cap runs until 31 December.
The cap limits the price paid for each unit of energy, not the total bill, so a home that uses more will still pay more. On the same day, VAT on household electricity was cut from 5% to nothing. This lasts until 31 March 2027, and gas still carries 5% VAT.
A typical household might save about £45 a year. The money expert Martin Lewis says the higher cap will take back much of this. Some reports give the rise as 3.6%, depending on how the VAT cut is counted.
levels.why: It decides how much families pay for heating and light this winter.

levels.headline: Your energy bill changed on 1 October
levels.body:
On 1 October, the limit on what energy firms can charge went up by 4%. This limit is called the price cap, and Ofgem sets it. For a typical home it is now £1,723 for a year. It went up because gas costs more to buy. The new cap runs until 31 December.
The cap is a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not on your whole bill. If you use more gas or electricity, you will still pay more.
The government also took VAT off electricity at home. VAT is a tax added to many things we buy. It was 5% and is now nothing, until 31 March 2027. Gas still has VAT. The average home might save about £45 in a year. But a money expert, Martin Lewis, says most of that is cancelled out by the higher cap.
levels.why: It affects how much families pay to keep their homes warm and lit.

levels.headline: Energy bills went up a little, and one tax went away
levels.body:
Energy firms are not allowed to charge more than a set price for each unit of gas or electricity. The set price is called the price cap. A group called Ofgem decides it. On 1 October it went up by 4%. This is because gas costs more to buy at the moment. For an average home, it means about £1,723 over a year.
The cap only limits the price of each unit. If a family uses more energy, they still pay more.
Also on 1 October, a tax called VAT was taken off electricity at home. It used to be 5%. That will last until 31 March 2027. An average home may save about £45 a year. A money expert called Martin Lewis says the higher price takes back a lot of that saving.
levels.why: It changes how much families pay for light and heat at home.

levels.headline: Why home energy costs a bit more, and one small tax is gone
levels.body:
Every home pays for gas and electricity. A group called Ofgem puts a limit on how much energy companies can charge for each unit they sell. That limit is called the price cap. On 1 October, the cap went up a little, by 4%. That is because the gas that energy firms buy has become more expensive.
For an average home, a year of energy now adds up to about £1,723. If a family uses more energy, they pay more.
On the same day, the government took a tax called VAT off electricity. A tax is money people pay to the government. The tax was 5% and is now nothing until March 2027. An average home might save about £45 over a year. A money expert, Martin Lewis, thinks the cap going up will cancel out much of the saving.
levels.why: It changes how much a family pays to keep the lights and heating on.

levels.headline: Bills for lights and heating changed this month
levels.body:
Your home uses energy for lights, heating and cooking. The company that sells it to you has to follow a rule about how much it can charge. The rule is called the price cap. This month, the cap went up a little, by about four pennies in every pound. It went up because gas costs more to buy.
For a typical home, a whole year of energy is about £1,723. That is a lot of money. Families who use more energy pay more.
There was some good news too. The government took a small tax off electricity. A tax is some money that people have to give to the government. It was five pennies in every £1 and now it is zero, for a while. A typical home could save about £45 a year. But a money expert says the higher cap takes much of that back.
levels.why: It changes how much families pay for light and heat.

levels.headline: Why the bill for lights and heating has changed
levels.body:
Every house needs energy to keep warm and to have lights. Companies sell it to families. A group called Ofgem makes a rule about how much the companies can ask for. This rule is called a cap, and it went up a little this month. That is because the gas the companies buy costs more.
But the government also made something cheaper. There was a small extra amount, called a tax, added to the cost of electricity. The government took it away for a while. A normal family might save a small amount each month. A money expert says the cap going up cancels out most of it.
So bills may stay about the same for electricity, and be a bit higher for gas. Families who use more energy will still pay more.
levels.why: It changes how much families pay for light and heat.

headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% with youth rate at 16.4% before new figures

terms.meaning: The share of people who are looking for work and available to start who do not have a job.
Pay after allowing for rising prices, which shows what it can actually buy.
People counted through tax records as being paid by an employer.

levels.headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% with youth rate at 16.4% before new figures
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July, according to the latest Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures, which means about 1.78 million people were out of work. That is up from 4.7% a year earlier but largely unchanged on the previous quarter. The ONS warns that caution is still needed when judging changes over time.
The rate for 16 to 24-year-olds was 16.4%, up from 14.3% a year before. Regular pay growth was 3.5% excluding bonuses and 3.9% including them, which after inflation is real growth of 0.8% and 1.1%. Payrolled employees, counted from tax records, fell by 84,000 over the year to July, even though the survey measure of employment rose by 243,000.
The next ONS labour market release is due on 20 October, and official monthly GDP figures for August are published on Thursday 15 October.
levels.why: Jobs and pay figures help decide whether the Bank of England raises or holds interest rates.

levels.headline: Unemployment steady at 4.9% but young people are finding it harder to get work
levels.body:
Unemployment stood at 4.9% in the three months to July, the Office for National Statistics reported, equal to roughly 1.78 million people. The rate is up from 4.7% a year earlier but has barely moved over the latest quarter. The ONS says its estimates should still be treated with care.
Among 16 to 24-year-olds the rate was 16.4%, compared with 14.3% a year before. Regular pay rose by 3.5% over the year excluding bonuses and 3.9% with them. After inflation that is a real increase of 0.8% and 1.1%. The number of payrolled employees, taken from tax records, fell by 84,000 over the year to July, while the survey measure of employment rose by 243,000, so the two sources disagree.
The next labour market figures arrive on 20 October, and August's monthly GDP figures are due on Thursday.
levels.why: It shows how a weak jobs market and slow pay growth are affecting households, especially the young.

levels.headline: Jobless rate steady at 4.9%, but one in six young people are unemployed
levels.body:
The unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July, says the Office for National Statistics. That is about 1.78 million people without a job who are looking for one. A year ago it was 4.7%, though it has hardly changed in the latest three months. The ONS says the figures still need to be read with care.
For people aged 16 to 24 the rate was 16.4%, up from 14.3% a year earlier. Pay is rising at 3.5% a year without bonuses and 3.9% with them. Once inflation is taken off, that is a rise of 0.8% and 1.1% in real terms.
Payrolled employees, based on tax records, were down 84,000 over the year, but a separate survey shows employment up by 243,000. The next figures come on 20 October.
levels.why: Weak hiring and slow pay growth leave many households, and especially young people, under pressure.

levels.headline: Unemployment is 4.9%, and it is higher for young people
levels.body:
About 1.78 million people in the UK were out of work in the three months to July. That is 4.9% of people who are able to work. A year ago it was 4.7%. Over the last three months it has not changed much, the Office for National Statistics says. But it adds that these numbers can be uncertain.
Young people have been hit harder. For those aged 16 to 24, the rate was 16.4%, which is up from 14.3% a year before. Pay is rising by 3.5% a year, or 3.9% if bonuses are counted. After prices are taken into account, that is a rise of about 1%.
Tax records show 84,000 fewer employees on payrolls than a year earlier. A survey, however, shows more people in work. The next jobs figures are out on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows that jobs are harder to find, especially for young people.

levels.headline: About 1.78 million people are out of work, and it is harder for the young
levels.body:
Unemployment in the UK was 4.9% in the three months to July. That means about 1.78 million people were looking for work and could not find it. A year earlier the rate was 4.7%, but over the last three months it has hardly changed. The Office for National Statistics says the figures should be read with care.
Young people are finding it hardest. For those aged 16 to 24, the rate was 16.4%, up from 14.3% a year before. Pay is rising at 3.5% a year without bonuses, which after rising prices is real growth of about 1%.
Tax records show 84,000 fewer employees on payrolls than a year earlier. The next jobs figures are due on 20 October.
levels.why: Jobs are harder to find, especially for young people, and pay is growing slowly.

levels.headline: Fewer jobs for young people, and pay is barely beating prices
levels.body:
The unemployment rate in the UK is 4.9%. This means that about 1.78 million people want a job and cannot find one. A year ago it was 4.7%, so it has gone up a little. The Office for National Statistics counts these numbers. It says they can be a bit uncertain.
It is harder for young people. Among those aged 16 to 24, 16.4% have no job. A year ago it was 14.3%. That means about one in six young people looking for work cannot find any.
Pay is going up by about 3.5% a year. Prices are going up too. After prices are counted, pay is only up by around 1%. That means wages buy only a little more than before. New figures are due on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows that jobs are scarce for young people and pay is growing slowly.

levels.headline: Many people are looking for a job and cannot find one
levels.body:
In the UK, almost 5 out of every 100 people who want to work do not have a job. That is 4.9%, or about 1.78 million people. A year ago it was a bit lower, at 4.7%. The people who count these things work for the Office for National Statistics.
Young people are finding it harder. For people aged 16 to 24, about 16 out of every 100 have no job. Last year it was about 14 out of every 100.
The good news is that pay is going up, by around 3.5% a year. The bad news is that prices are also going up. So the extra pay only buys about 1% more than before. Tax records also show fewer workers on company payrolls than a year ago. More figures come out on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows that jobs are hard to find for young people and pay barely stretches further.

levels.headline: Jobs are hard to find, especially for young people
levels.body:
Lots of grown-ups go to work and get paid. But some people want a job and cannot find one. Right now, in the UK, that is about 1.78 million people. Out of every 100 people who could work, about five are looking for a job and have not got one.
Young people between 16 and 24 are finding it hardest. About 16 out of every 100 of them cannot find a job. A year ago it was about 14 out of every 100.
Workers' pay is going up a little, by about 3.5% in a year. But the prices of things in shops have gone up too. So workers can buy only a tiny bit more than before. A group called the Office for National Statistics counts all this. It will share new numbers on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows that many people struggle to find work, and pay does not stretch far.

levels.headline: Some people cannot find a job, and young people find it hardest
levels.body:
Most grown-ups work to earn money. Some people want to work but cannot find a job. In the UK, about five people out of every hundred who want a job do not have one. That is a lot of people. It is about one million seven hundred and eighty thousand.
It is hardest for young people. Between the ages of 16 and 24, about one in six cannot find a job. A year ago it was fewer.
Workers who do have jobs are being paid a bit more than last year. But things in shops cost more too. So their extra pay only buys a tiny bit more than before. The people who count all these numbers are called the Office for National Statistics. They will share new numbers on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows that jobs are hard to find, especially for young people.

levels.headline: Why some people cannot find a job right now
levels.body:
Imagine lots of people lining up for a few jobs. That is a bit like what is happening in the UK now. Many people want a job but cannot get one. Out of every hundred people who could work, about five are in this situation.
It is hardest for young people, like your older brothers and sisters. About one in six young people who want a job cannot find one.
There is another problem. People with jobs are paid a bit more than last year. But shop prices have gone up as well. So the extra pay is a bit like finding an extra penny in your pocket when the sweets cost two pennies more. Some people count all of this and tell everyone on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows that jobs are hard to find for young people and pay does not go far.

headline: YouGov poll puts Labour, Conservatives and Reform within three points

terms.meaning: A poll question asking how people would vote if a general election were held tomorrow.
The range within which a poll result could differ from the true figure because only a sample is asked.
Shorthand for the UK Parliament, and so for UK-wide elections.

levels.headline: YouGov poll puts Labour, Conservatives and Reform within three points
levels.body:
A YouGov poll for The Times and Sky News, carried out on 11 and 12 October, put Labour on 24%, the Conservatives on 23% and Reform UK on 21%. The Liberal Democrats were on 12%, the Greens on 11%, the SNP on 3%, Restore Britain on 2% and Plaid Cymru on 1%.
Labour fell three points from YouGov's 4 and 5 October poll, when it had 27%, and the Conservatives rose three points. YouGov says the three leading parties are all within the margin of error of one another. The 23% is the Conservatives' highest on its tracker since January 2025, and Reform's 21% is its joint-lowest this parliament.
Other pollsters differ. Opinium on 7 October had Labour on 29%, Reform on 23% and the Conservatives on 20%, with a modest Conservative rise after their party conference. Averages of recent polls still show Labour narrowly ahead.
levels.why: It shows that no party has a secure lead and the race is tight.

levels.headline: Labour, Conservatives and Reform in a three-way tie, says YouGov poll
levels.body:
The latest YouGov poll for The Times and Sky News, taken on 11 and 12 October, found Labour on 24%, the Conservatives on 23% and Reform UK on 21%. The Liberal Democrats had 12%, the Greens 11%, the SNP 3%, Restore Britain 2% and Plaid Cymru 1%.
Compared with the poll of 4 and 5 October, Labour is down three points from 27% and the Conservatives are up three. YouGov says all three of the leading parties are within the margin of error of each other. The Conservative figure is their best on its tracker since January 2025, while Reform's is joint-lowest this parliament.
One poll is not the whole picture. Opinium, on 7 October, had Labour on 29%, Reform on 23% and the Conservatives on 20%, and averages of recent polls put Labour a few points ahead.
levels.why: It suggests no party has a secure lead, which affects how the government and its rivals behave.

levels.headline: Poll shows a very close race between Labour, Conservatives and Reform
levels.body:
A new YouGov poll for The Times and Sky News gives Labour 24%, the Conservatives 23% and Reform UK 21%. It was carried out on 11 and 12 October. The Liberal Democrats are on 12% and the Greens on 11%.
Labour has dropped three points since YouGov's poll a week earlier, when it had 27%. The Conservatives have risen three points. YouGov points out that the three biggest parties are all within the margin of error, so the true order could be different. The Conservatives' 23% is their highest on YouGov's tracker since January 2025. Reform's 21% is its lowest this parliament, level with an earlier result.
Other polls show a different picture. Opinium, on 7 October, had Labour on 29%. Overall averages still show Labour narrowly in front, with Reform second and the Conservatives third.
levels.why: It shows how unsettled British politics is, and how quickly party support can change.

levels.headline: Three parties are almost level in a new opinion poll
levels.body:
A company called YouGov asked people how they would vote if an election were held now. The poll was done on 11 and 12 October for The Times and Sky News. Labour got 24%, the Conservatives got 23% and Reform UK got 21%. The Liberal Democrats got 12% and the Greens got 11%.
A week earlier, Labour had 27%. So it has lost three points, while the Conservatives have gained three. YouGov says the top three are so close that the real order could be different, because polls only ask a sample of people. The Conservatives' score is their best since January 2025.
Other pollsters get different results. One called Opinium had Labour on 29% on 7 October. When many polls are averaged, Labour is still slightly ahead.
levels.why: It shows that no party has a clear lead, and that opinion can change fast.

levels.headline: Labour, the Conservatives and Reform are very close in a new poll
levels.body:
A poll asks a sample of people how they would vote if an election were held now. The company YouGov did this on 11 and 12 October for The Times and Sky News. Labour got 24%, the Conservatives 23% and Reform UK 21%. The Liberal Democrats got 12% and the Greens 11%.
A week earlier Labour had 27%, so it has lost three points, while the Conservatives gained three. YouGov says the top three are all within the margin of error. That means the true order could be different, because only some people were asked.
The Conservatives' 23% is their best on YouGov's tracker since January 2025. Other pollsters, such as Opinium, have shown Labour further ahead, and averages still put it narrowly in front.
levels.why: It shows that no party has a secure lead.

levels.headline: Labour, the Conservatives and Reform are nearly level in a new poll
levels.body:
Pollsters ask people which party they would vote for if there was an election tomorrow. The company YouGov did this on 11 and 12 October. Labour came out on 24%, the Conservatives on 23% and Reform UK on 21%. The Liberal Democrats had 12% and the Greens had 11%.
One week earlier Labour was on 27%. So Labour fell by three points and the Conservatives went up by three. YouGov says the top three are so close that the true order could be different. A poll only asks some people, not everyone, so it is not exact.
Other polls give other answers. A company called Opinium found Labour on 29% on 7 October. Putting many polls together, Labour is still a little bit ahead of Reform and the Conservatives.
levels.why: It shows that no party has a safe lead, and polls can change fast.

levels.headline: A new poll shows three parties neck and neck
levels.body:
A poll is when people are asked who they would vote for. A company called YouGov asked people on 11 and 12 October. About 24 out of every 100 said Labour. About 23 said the Conservatives. About 21 said Reform UK. Smaller numbers said the Liberal Democrats or the Greens.
A week earlier, more people said Labour. It was 27 out of every 100. So Labour has lost a little. The Conservatives have gained a little.
The three parties are so close that YouGov says any of them could really be in front. This is because a poll only asks some people, not everybody in the country. Other polls show Labour doing better. Many experts add the polls together to get a better picture. That still shows Labour a bit ahead.
levels.why: It shows that nobody has a safe lead, and people can change their minds.

levels.headline: Who might win if there was an election? It is very close
levels.body:
A poll is a way of asking lots of people a question to see what they think. In this one, a company asked people which party they would vote for. This was on 11 and 12 October. About a quarter said Labour. Almost as many said the Conservatives. A bit fewer said Reform UK.
The numbers were very close. A week earlier Labour was ahead by more. The company that asked, YouGov, says the top three parties are so close that any one of them could really be in front. That is because it only asked some people, not everyone in the country.
Other polls have shown different numbers. When experts mix many polls together, Labour is still a little bit ahead. In real elections, the votes of everyone count.
levels.why: It shows that nobody has a safe lead.

levels.headline: A race where three teams are nearly level
levels.body:
Imagine a race with three runners who are very close together. A new poll says British politics looks a bit like that. A poll is a way of asking lots of people who they would vote for. The company YouGov asked on 11 and 12 October.
About 24 out of every 100 people said Labour. About 23 said the Conservatives. About 21 said Reform UK. These are very close. A week before, Labour was a bit further ahead.
YouGov says that the three are so close that anybody could really be in front. The poll only asked some people, not everyone. Other polls show Labour doing better. Nobody knows yet who would win. Real votes only happen at elections, when grown-ups choose a party.
levels.why: It shows that nobody is far ahead.

levels.headline: Who do grown-ups want to be in charge? It is a close race
levels.body:
In class, you might vote for a favourite game. Grown-ups vote for who runs the country. Before a vote, a company asks some people who they would pick. This is called a poll. A company called YouGov asked grown-ups on 11 and 12 October.
Three groups, called parties, were nearly level. They are called Labour, the Conservatives and Reform UK. It was like three teams all just a point or two apart at the end of a match.
A week before, Labour was a bit more ahead. Now the others have caught up a little. The company says it only asked some people, so the real result could be different. The real vote is only held at an election.
levels.why: It shows that nobody is far ahead yet.

headline: IMF lifts 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but warns of a split outlook

terms.meaning: The International Monetary Fund, a global body that lends to governments and publishes economic forecasts.
Countries that buy more oil and gas than they produce.
An informed estimate of what will happen, which can turn out wrong.

levels.headline: IMF lifts 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but warns of a split outlook
levels.body:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on 13 October that it expects the world economy to grow by 3.1% in 2026, up slightly from the 3.0% it forecast in July, and by 3.4% in 2027. Global growth was 3.5% in 2025. The figures come from its October World Economic Outlook, released at its annual meetings in Bangkok.
The IMF expects the United States to grow by 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, and the eurozone by 1.1%. Growth in China is expected to slow, mainly because of weak domestic demand. Global inflation is forecast at 4.7% this year and 4.1% next year.
The IMF describes a split outlook. Investment in artificial intelligence is lifting some economies, while the energy shock from the war involving Iran hits energy importers and low-income countries hardest. Its forecast assumes oil averages about $96 a barrel and that shipments through the Strait of Hormuz resume by March.
levels.why: It sets the backdrop for budgets and interest-rate decisions in the UK and around the world.

levels.headline: IMF nudges global growth forecast up to 3.1%, with a warning about the energy shock
levels.body:
The IMF has raised its 2026 forecast for global growth to 3.1%, from 3.0% in July, and expects 3.4% in 2027. The figures, published on 13 October in the World Economic Outlook at the Bangkok meetings, compare with 3.5% growth in 2025.
US growth is forecast to stay steady at 2.3% in 2026 and 2027, while the eurozone is expected to manage 1.1%. China is expected to slow because of weak domestic demand. The IMF puts global inflation at 4.7% this year, easing to 4.1% in 2027.
It calls the outlook split. Heavy investment in artificial intelligence supports some economies, but countries that import energy and poorer nations suffer most from the higher energy costs linked to the war. The forecast assumes oil averages around $96 a barrel and that Hormuz shipping resumes by March, so a longer disruption would hurt growth further.
levels.why: It shows how the Middle East war is weighing on the world economy even as AI spending helps.

levels.headline: IMF raises 2026 growth forecast slightly but says gains are uneven
levels.body:
The International Monetary Fund now expects the world economy to grow by 3.1% in 2026. In July it had said 3.0%. For 2027 it expects 3.4%. Last year the figure was 3.5%. The numbers were published on 13 October in Bangkok.
The IMF expects the US economy to grow by 2.3% in both years and the eurozone to grow by 1.1%. China is likely to slow because people there are spending less. Worldwide, prices are forecast to rise by 4.7% this year and 4.1% next year.
The IMF says the outlook is split. Spending on artificial intelligence is helping some countries. But countries that buy lots of oil and gas, and low-income countries, are suffering from the energy shock caused by the war. The forecast assumes oil will average about $96 a barrel and that ships will pass through the Strait of Hormuz again by March.
levels.why: It shows which parts of the world economy are coping and which are struggling.

levels.headline: World economy to grow 3.1% this year, says the IMF
levels.body:
The IMF, a global body that lends to governments and studies the world economy, has updated its forecast. It now expects the world's economy to grow by 3.1% this year. In July, it said 3.0%. Next year it expects 3.4%. These are estimates, so they can turn out wrong.
It thinks the US economy will grow 2.3% this year and the eurozone 1.1%. China is expected to slow down because its people are spending less. Prices around the world are expected to go up by 4.7% this year.
The IMF says the picture is uneven. Money going into artificial intelligence is helping some countries. Countries that have to buy lots of oil and gas are being hurt by the war and its high energy prices, and so are poorer countries. The IMF assumes that oil will cost about $96 a barrel and that ships can use the Strait of Hormuz again by March.
levels.why: It shows who gains and who loses as the world copes with high energy prices.

levels.headline: The IMF expects the world economy to grow by 3.1% this year
levels.body:
The International Monetary Fund, a global body that publishes economic forecasts, now expects the world economy to grow by 3.1% in 2026. In July it said 3.0%. For 2027 it expects 3.4%, and last year's growth was 3.5%. A forecast is an informed estimate, so it can turn out wrong.
It expects the United States to grow by 2.3% and the eurozone by 1.1%, while China slows because people there are spending less. Prices around the world are forecast to rise by 4.7% this year.
The IMF says the picture is uneven. Investment in artificial intelligence helps some countries, but those that must buy lots of oil and gas, and poorer countries, are hit by the energy shock. The forecast assumes oil averages about $96 a barrel and that ships use the Strait of Hormuz again by March.
levels.why: It shows who gains and who loses as the world copes with dear energy.

levels.headline: A world forecast: slow growth and high prices
levels.body:
The International Monetary Fund, or IMF, is a group that helps countries with money problems. It also makes guesses about how the world economy will do. This week it said it expects the economy to grow by 3.1% this year. That means all the things countries make and sell added together will grow a little. It said 3.0% in July. For next year it guesses 3.4%.
It expects US growth of 2.3% and 1.1% for countries using the euro. China is expected to slow down. Prices around the world are expected to rise by 4.7% this year.
The IMF says some countries are doing better than others. Spending on artificial intelligence is helping some. But places that buy lots of oil and gas are being hurt by high prices because of the war. These are only guesses.
levels.why: It shows that high energy prices hurt countries that have to buy oil and gas.

levels.headline: The world economy is growing slowly, and prices are still rising
levels.body:
A group called the IMF helps countries with money matters. It has made a guess about the world economy. It says the world will make and sell about 3.1% more things this year than last year. That is a small rise. Last year the rise was a bit bigger, at 3.5%.
The IMF also thinks prices will go up by 4.7% around the world this year. That means things in shops cost more. The war in the Middle East is part of the reason, because it has made oil and gas expensive.
Some countries are doing better. New computer technology, called artificial intelligence, is helping some of them. Countries that have to buy lots of oil and gas are doing worse. So are poorer countries. The IMF says its guess depends on ships being able to use an important sea route, the Strait of Hormuz, by March.
levels.why: It shows that war can make life more expensive all around the world.

levels.headline: The IMF's guess about how the world's money is doing
levels.body:
The world has an economy. This means all the buying and selling that people do. A group called the IMF tries to guess how it will go. This week it said it will grow by about 3.1% this year. That is a small amount of growth.
Prices are also going up. The IMF thinks they will rise by 4.7% this year around the world. That means the things we buy cost more. Part of the reason is a war in the Middle East. It has made oil and gas cost more.
Some countries are doing better than others. Some are getting a boost from new computer helpers, called artificial intelligence. Countries that have to buy lots of oil and gas are finding it harder. The IMF is only guessing. If ships cannot sail through an important sea path, things could be worse.
levels.why: It shows that a war far away can make things cost more for everyone.

levels.headline: How is the world's money doing? Not too bad, but prices are up
levels.body:
All the countries in the world buy and sell things. This is called the world economy. A group of money experts, called the IMF, has made a guess about it. They think it will grow a little bit this year. That is good news, but it is a small amount.
But prices are going up. Things that people buy cost more than before. Part of the reason is a war in the Middle East. It has made fuel cost more. Fuel is used to move cars, ships and planes.
Some countries are finding it easier than others. Countries that have to buy lots of fuel are finding it hard. The experts say that if the war goes on for longer, it could be worse. These are guesses, so they might be wrong.
levels.why: It shows that a war far away can make things cost more at home.

levels.headline: Why things cost more around the world
levels.body:
Think about a big school tuck shop for the whole world. Every country buys and sells things there. Some money experts, called the IMF, have been thinking about how it will go this year. They think the shop will do a little bit better than last year, but only a little.
They also think the prices will go up. A war in the Middle East has made fuel cost more. Fuel moves things from place to place, so almost everything gets a bit dearer.
Some countries can cope better than others. Countries that have to buy a lot of fuel find it hard. The experts say these are only guesses. If ships can use an important sea path again soon, things could get better.
levels.why: It shows why a war far away can raise prices at home.

headline: Brent crude holds near $106 as ships are struck in the Strait of Hormuz

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil, quoted in dollars per barrel.
A narrow sea route between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped.
The standard unit for oil, about 159 litres.

levels.headline: Brent crude holds near $106 as ships are struck in the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, traded around $106 a barrel on Wednesday, up 63 cents or 0.6% to $106.32, after two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials told Reuters they are using new tactics to target ships passing through the waterway.
The price has moved sharply in recent days. Brent rose above $105 on 8 October on concerns that the war involving Iran could escalate, and it climbed again after attacks on tankers. Oil fell on Monday on hopes that Russia and Ukraine would agree an energy ceasefire, and it slipped back on Tuesday after topping $106.
Sources disagree about shipping. One live tracker describes the strait as effectively closed to commercial traffic, while a US State Department spokesperson said oil shipments have passed pre-conflict levels, excluding Iranian oil, which is under a US blockade.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating, transport costs and inflation almost everywhere.

levels.headline: Oil near $106 a barrel after fresh attacks on ships near Hormuz
levels.body:
Brent crude was trading at around $106 a barrel on Wednesday morning, rising 63 cents, or 0.6%, to $106.32 after two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials told Reuters they are deploying new tactics to hit ships using the waterway.
Prices have been jumpy. Brent topped $105 on 8 October as President Trump was reported to be weighing a return to major combat operations in Iran, and it fell on Monday on hopes of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire. It eased again on Tuesday after passing $106.
Accounts of traffic through Hormuz conflict. A live tracker says the strait is effectively shut to commercial shipping, but the US State Department says shipments have exceeded pre-conflict levels once Iranian oil, which is blockaded, is excluded. The IMF's new forecast assumes oil averages about $96 a barrel this year.
levels.why: High oil prices keep inflation up, which makes interest-rate cuts less likely.

levels.headline: Oil prices climb to about $106 as two ships are hit near the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main global oil benchmark, was about $106 a barrel on Wednesday. It rose 63 cents to $106.32 after two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route through which much of the world's oil travels. Iranian officials told Reuters they are using new tactics against ships.
Oil has swung up and down this week. It went above $105 on 8 October because of fears that the war with Iran could get worse. It dropped on Monday on hopes of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, then fell slightly on Tuesday.
There is disagreement about how much oil is moving. A tracking website says the strait is effectively closed to commercial ships. The US State Department says shipments are above pre-war levels, not counting Iranian oil, which the US is blocking.
levels.why: Dearer oil raises fuel and transport costs, and can push up prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil costs about $106 a barrel after ships are attacked
levels.body:
Oil is priced in barrels. A barrel is about 159 litres. The main world price, called Brent crude, was about $106 a barrel on Wednesday. It had gone up by 63 cents. Two ships were hit in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of sea that a lot of the world's oil has to pass through. Iran told the news agency Reuters that it is using new methods to attack ships.
The price has jumped around this week. It went over $105 on 8 October as people feared the war with Iran might get worse. It fell on Monday because people hoped Russia and Ukraine would stop attacking energy sites.
Nobody agrees on how many ships are getting through. One tracking website says the route is nearly closed. The US government says more oil is moving than before the war, apart from Iranian oil.
levels.why: Higher oil prices make fuel and many other things dearer.

levels.headline: Oil is about $106 a barrel after ships are hit in the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
The main world oil price, Brent crude, was about $106 a barrel on Wednesday. It rose 63 cents after two ships were struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route that carries a large share of the world's oil. Iranian officials told Reuters they are using new tactics against ships.
The price has swung this week. It went above $105 on 8 October, fell on Monday when people hoped Russia and Ukraine would stop attacking energy sites, and eased on Tuesday after passing $106.
People disagree about how much oil is moving. One tracking website says the strait is effectively closed, while the US says shipments are above pre-war levels without Iranian oil, which it blockades. Dearer oil means dearer fuel.
levels.why: Dearer oil feeds into petrol, transport costs and prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Why oil is dear: ships have been attacked near a key sea route
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid that is turned into petrol, diesel and other fuels. It is sold by the barrel, and the main world price is called Brent. On Wednesday a barrel cost about $106. That is a lot. It went up after two ships were hit in the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow sea route that lots of the world's oil ships have to use.
Iran told a news agency that it has new ways to attack ships. That makes shipping companies nervous, and oil gets dearer when fewer ships can be sure of getting through.
The price has gone up and down this week. It fell when people hoped Russia and Ukraine would stop attacking each other's energy sites. People disagree about how many ships are getting through the strait now.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol, heating and goods in shops can cost more too.

levels.headline: Oil is expensive because of trouble at sea
levels.body:
Oil is used to make fuel for cars, lorries, ships and planes. A barrel of oil now costs about $106. That is very expensive. It went up a little on Wednesday because two ships were hit in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. A lot of the world's oil has to go through this route.
Iran, a country in the Middle East, says it is trying new ways to attack ships. This makes ship owners worried. When they worry, they may not send ships, and oil gets even more expensive.
The price has gone up and down this week. It fell on Monday when people hoped two other countries, Russia and Ukraine, would stop attacking each other's energy sites. Different people say different things about how many ships are getting through.
levels.why: Dearer oil makes petrol and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: Why fuel is so expensive right now
levels.body:
Cars, lorries and ships use fuel. Fuel is made from oil. Right now, oil costs a lot of money. A barrel costs about $106. A barrel is a big container.
Oil is expensive because ships carrying it have been attacked. They have to go through a narrow sea path called the Strait of Hormuz. Two ships were hit there this week. A country called Iran says it has new ways to attack ships. This makes people worried that there will be less oil.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more. Things in shops can cost more too, because lorries need fuel. The price went up and down this week as people heard different news.
levels.why: Dearer oil makes petrol and shop prices go up.

levels.headline: Why petrol and other things cost more
levels.body:
Cars and lorries need fuel to move. Fuel is made from oil. Right now oil costs a lot. The ships that carry oil have to sail along a narrow sea path. Some ships have been attacked there this week.
When ships are attacked, people worry that there will not be enough oil. When people worry, they pay more for it. It is a bit like when there is only one toy left in the shop and everybody wants it. The price goes up.
When oil is dear, petrol is dear too. Lorries need petrol to bring food and toys to the shops. So the price of lots of things can go up. The price of oil went up and down a bit this week, depending on the news.
levels.why: Dearer oil makes petrol and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: Why things in shops can cost more
levels.body:
Lorries bring food and toys to the shops. They need fuel to do this. Fuel comes from a thing called oil. Oil comes in big ships. The ships sail on the sea.
This week, some ships were hit by attackers on a narrow path through the sea. People worried that there might not be enough oil. When people worry about running out, the price goes up. It is like when everyone in the playground wants the same ball.
So oil costs a lot now. That makes fuel cost more, and then shop prices can go up as well. Grown-ups hope the fighting will stop so ships can sail safely and the prices can come down again.
levels.why: It explains why many things cost more when oil costs more.

headline: US inflation data due as the Fed weighs another rate rise

terms.meaning: The US central bank, which sets the main US interest rate.
The Consumer Prices Index, a measure of how much prices have risen over a year.
The interest rate the US government pays to borrow by selling bonds.

levels.headline: US inflation data due as the Fed weighs another rate rise
levels.body:
The United States publishes its September inflation figures today, and economists expect the annual rate to rise to between 3.6% and 3.7%, from 3.4% in August. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, is expected to stay near 2.4% to 2.5%.
The Federal Reserve raised its target range by a quarter of a point to 3.75% to 4.00% on 16 September, in a 12 to 0 vote, its first increase since July 2023. Minutes published on 7 October showed officials expect another rise but gave no clear timing. Markets put the chance of a rise at the next meeting on 28 October at roughly 20%, and the odds of a December increase are put near 70%.
The 10-year Treasury yield was around 5.22% on Tuesday, a level not seen in more than two decades, and US stocks were broadly flat to slightly lower as chip shares fell and oil swung.
levels.why: US interest rates and bond yields influence borrowing costs and markets around the world, including in the UK.

levels.headline: Fed keeps the door open to more rate rises as US inflation figures arrive
levels.body:
September's US consumer price figures are due today. Forecasters expect annual inflation of 3.6% to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August, with core inflation steady at roughly 2.4% to 2.5%. Higher energy costs linked to the Middle East war are the main driver.
The Federal Reserve lifted its target range to 3.75% to 4.00% on 16 September by a unanimous 12 to 0 vote, its first rise since July 2023. The minutes of that meeting, released on 7 October, said officials see another increase coming, without saying when. Traders see only about a one in five chance of a rise on 28 October but around a 70% chance by December.
The 10-year Treasury yield stood at about 5.22% on Tuesday. US shares were little changed to slightly lower that day, with chip stocks falling and oil prices volatile.
levels.why: What the Fed does affects the cost of borrowing worldwide and the value of savings and investments.

levels.headline: US inflation figures today as the Federal Reserve signals more rate rises
levels.body:
The United States is due to publish its September inflation figures today. Economists expect prices to be 3.6% to 3.7% higher than a year ago, compared with 3.4% in August. When food and energy are left out, the figure is expected to be about 2.4% to 2.5%.
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a point on 16 September. The range is now 3.75% to 4.00%. All 12 voters agreed. Minutes released on 7 October show that officials expect to raise rates again, but did not say when. Traders think a rise on 28 October is unlikely, but they put the chance of one by December at around 70%.
The yield on 10-year US government bonds was about 5.22% on Tuesday. Share prices were roughly flat.
levels.why: It affects borrowing costs for governments, firms and families well beyond the United States.

levels.headline: US inflation numbers are due, and interest rates may rise again
levels.body:
Today the United States will say how fast prices rose in September. Experts think prices were 3.6% to 3.7% higher than a year ago. In August it was 3.4%. That would mean prices are rising a little faster.
The US central bank is called the Federal Reserve. It raised its main interest rate by a small step on 16 September, to between 3.75% and 4.00%. This was the first rise since July 2023. Notes from the meeting, shared on 7 October, say officials expect another rise but did not say when. Traders think it is unlikely at the next meeting, on 28 October, but fairly likely by December.
The US government's cost of borrowing for ten years was about 5.22% on Tuesday. That is the highest in more than twenty years. Share prices were around the same as the day before.
levels.why: It matters because US rates affect borrowing and savings in many countries.

levels.headline: American prices and interest rates: what to watch today
levels.body:
Every month the United States shares a number showing how fast prices rise. Today it shares the number for September. Experts guess that prices are about 3.6% to 3.7% higher than a year ago. In August, it was 3.4%. So prices may be rising a bit faster.
The US has a central bank, called the Federal Reserve. It sets the main interest rate. This is the price of borrowing money. On 16 September it raised the rate a little, to between 3.75% and 4.00%. It was the first rise since 2023. The Fed's notes say officials expect to raise it again, but they did not say when.
Governments also borrow. The US government pays about 5.22% to borrow for ten years. That is very high compared with the last twenty years.
levels.why: US rates affect borrowing and savings around the world.

levels.headline: Will American interest rates go up again?
levels.body:
Today the United States will say how much prices went up last month. Experts think prices are rising a bit faster than before. A year ago, prices were lower, and now they are about 3.6% to 3.7% higher. In August the number was 3.4%.
The US has a bank for banks, called the Federal Reserve. It sets an important interest rate. That is the price of borrowing money. In September it put the rate up a little. The new level is between 3.75% and 4.00%. People at the Fed said they think another rise will be needed. They did not say when.
The US government also borrows money. Right now it has to pay about 5.22% on a ten-year loan. This is very high. It is the highest for over twenty years.
levels.why: US rates affect borrowing costs in many other countries.

levels.headline: Prices and interest rates in America
levels.body:
When prices go up a lot, it can be hard for families. The United States counts how fast prices go up. Today it will share the new count. Experts think prices are up about 3.6% to 3.7% over a year. That is a little faster than before.
There is a bank in America that looks after the country's money. It is called the Federal Reserve. It sets an interest rate. That is the extra cost of borrowing money. In September it made the rate a bit higher. Higher rates help slow price rises down. People at the bank said they think they may need to raise it again.
The government also has to pay interest when it borrows. It is paying a lot at the moment, more than for twenty years.
levels.why: US rates affect borrowing around the world.

levels.headline: Why America might make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
If lots of people want the same thing, the price goes up. This is what happens with prices in shops. A country counts how much prices have gone up in a year. America will tell us today. Experts think prices went up by about 3.6% or 3.7% in a year. That is a bit more than before.
America has a big bank for its money. It is called the Federal Reserve. Last month it made the cost of borrowing a little higher. It does this to help stop prices from going up too fast. People at the bank think they may have to do it again. They have not said when.
The government pays extra when it borrows, too. At the moment it pays a lot.
levels.why: It shows that high prices can make borrowing cost more.

levels.headline: Why prices go up and what the bank can do
levels.body:
When the shop makes lollipops cost more, you can buy fewer. Prices in America have been going up. Today we will find out by how much. Grown-ups think it is a bit more than before.
America has a special bank in charge of money. It can make borrowing cost more. This can help to stop prices going up so fast. Last month it did that, a little. Now people think it might do it again.
When borrowing costs more, people buy fewer big things. Then shops may not need to make their prices higher. It is like a seesaw. It can take a long time to work.
levels.why: Borrowing costs affect families, shops and governments.

levels.headline: What makes prices go up, and how a bank tries to help
levels.body:
Imagine the tuck shop makes sweets more expensive each week. Your pocket money buys fewer. The same thing happens in America. Prices have been going up. Today we will find out how much.
America has a big bank that looks after the country's money. When prices go up too fast, the bank can make borrowing cost more. Then people borrow less and spend less. The shops may then stop raising prices. This is a bit like turning down the heat when a room is too hot.
The bank did this last month. Some people think it may do it again. Nobody knows for sure yet.
levels.why: Borrowing costs affect families, shops and governments.

headline: ECB expected to hold rates at 2.5% on 29 October after two hikes

terms.meaning: The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro.
The ECB's main policy rate, paid on money banks leave with it overnight.
Price rises excluding volatile items such as energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.

levels.headline: ECB expected to hold rates at 2.5% on 29 October after two hikes
levels.body:
Markets expect the European Central Bank (ECB) to leave interest rates unchanged at its next meeting on 29 October, with pricing implying roughly an 87% chance of a hold. The deposit facility rate stands at 2.5% after a quarter-point rise on 10 September, the second increase since the ECB first moved in three years on 11 June. The main refinancing rate is 2.65%.
The hikes were a response to an energy shock linked to the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up eurozone inflation. ECB staff projections put headline inflation at about 3% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, eased to 2.4% in August from 2.5%.
The IMF forecast this week that the eurozone will grow by just 1.1% in 2026, which leaves the ECB balancing weak growth against energy-led inflation.
levels.why: It shows central banks on both sides of the Channel are fighting energy-driven price rises.

levels.headline: ECB tipped to pause after two rate rises this year
levels.body:
The European Central Bank is expected to keep rates on hold when it meets on 29 October. Market pricing suggests an 87% chance of no change. Its deposit rate is 2.5% after a quarter-point increase on 10 September, the second since June, when it moved for the first time in three years. The main refinancing rate is 2.65%.
The ECB raised rates because the energy shock from the Middle East conflict has driven up inflation. Its staff expect headline inflation of about 3% this year, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items, slipped to 2.4% in August from 2.5%.
Growth is weak. The IMF now sees the eurozone expanding by only 1.1% this year, so the ECB must weigh slow growth against the risk that high prices stick.
levels.why: It affects borrowing costs across Europe and the pound's exchange rate against the euro.

levels.headline: European Central Bank likely to hold rates after raising them twice
levels.body:
The European Central Bank (ECB) is expected to leave interest rates alone at its next meeting on 29 October. Markets think there is about an 87% chance of this. The ECB's main rate, the deposit rate, is 2.5% after it went up by a quarter of a point on 10 September. That was the second rise since June.
The ECB raised rates because energy prices linked to the Middle East war have pushed up inflation in the countries that use the euro. Its experts expect prices to rise by about 3% this year. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, fell slightly to 2.4% in August.
The economy is not growing fast. The IMF expects only 1.1% growth in the eurozone this year, so the ECB has to balance high prices against weak growth.
levels.why: It shows how energy prices are pushing central banks to raise rates.

levels.headline: Europe's central bank is expected to pause its rate rises
levels.body:
The European Central Bank, or ECB, sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro. It is expected to leave rates as they are on 29 October. Markets think that is about 87% likely. Its main rate is 2.5%. It went up by a quarter of a point on 10 September. That was the second rise this year, after one in June.
