The ECB raised rates because energy costs have pushed prices up. Energy costs have risen because of the war in the Middle East. Experts at the bank think prices will rise by about 3% this year. Without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose by 2.4% in the year to August.
The euro area is not growing quickly. The IMF thinks it will grow by 1.1% this year.
levels.why: It shows that high energy prices are affecting central banks across Europe.

levels.headline: Europe's central bank is expected to pause after raising rates twice
levels.body:
Many European countries use the euro and share a bank, the European Central Bank. It sets the main interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. That rate is 2.5% after rises in June and September. Markets think there is about an 87% chance it stays the same at the next meeting, on 29 October.
The bank raised rates because energy prices, pushed up by the war in the Middle East, made prices rise faster. Its experts expect prices to rise by about 3% this year. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.4% in August.
Growth is weak. The IMF expects only 1.1% for the eurozone this year, so the bank must weigh high prices against a slow economy.
levels.why: Energy prices are making central banks across Europe raise rates.

levels.headline: Europe's bank may keep interest rates the same
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the same money, called the euro. They share a bank, called the European Central Bank. It decides how expensive it is to borrow money. Its main rate is 2.5%. It raised the rate in June and again in September. People think it will not change it on 29 October. The chance is about 87%.
Why did it raise rates? Prices went up because energy costs more. That is because of a war in the Middle East. The bank wants prices to stay steady. Its experts think prices will go up by about 3% this year.
But the countries are not growing very fast. A group called the IMF thinks growth will be only 1.1%. So the bank has to take care. Higher rates could slow things down even more.
levels.why: It shows that energy prices affect interest rates in Europe too.

levels.headline: Europe's bank has put up interest rates twice this year
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe share the same money, the euro. They also share a bank, which sets an interest rate. This is the cost of borrowing money. The rate is 2.5%. The bank put it up in June and then again in September. Most people think it will leave it alone at the next meeting, on 29 October.
It raised the rate because prices went up. Energy, like oil and gas, costs more now because of a war. The bank thinks prices will go up by about 3% this year. It wants to stop prices from rising too fast.
But the economy is not growing very quickly. So the bank has to be careful. If borrowing costs too much, businesses may stop growing.
levels.why: Energy prices affect interest rates in Europe too.

levels.headline: Why Europe's bank changed interest rates
levels.body:
Some countries in Europe share a type of money called the euro. They have a shared bank that looks after it. When prices in shops go up too fast, the bank can make borrowing cost more. This slows spending down. It did this in June and again in September. Now the cost is 2.5%.
Prices went up because fuel and gas cost more. That is because of a war far away. The bank thinks prices will go up by about 3% this year.
People now think the bank will leave the cost the same at its next meeting, on 29 October. The countries are not growing fast, so the bank wants to be careful. Making borrowing dearer could slow things even more.
levels.why: It shows that fuel prices affect interest rates in Europe.

levels.headline: The bank that looks after money for lots of countries
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the same coins and notes, called the euro. They share a bank to look after them. The bank sets how much extra people pay when they borrow. This extra is called interest.
When shop prices go up too quickly, the bank can raise the interest. Then people spend less, and prices may stop going up so fast. The bank did this twice this year. Prices had been rising because fuel and gas cost more.
Now most people think the bank will wait and see at its next meeting, on 29 October. It does not want to do too much and slow down the shops and factories.
levels.why: It shows how fuel prices affect borrowing in Europe.

levels.headline: A bank for lots of countries decides what to do
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe all use the same money. They have one big bank to look after it. The bank decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money. This is a bit like paying a little more to borrow a toy from a friend.
Prices in the shops had been going up because fuel cost more. So the bank made borrowing cost a bit more, two times. This is meant to help stop prices rising.
Now the grown-ups at the bank are probably going to wait and see. They will decide on 29 October. They do not want to make things too hard for shops and factories.
levels.why: It shows how a bank tries to keep prices steady.

headline: Hormuz attacks continue as US and Iran remain at a stalemate

terms.meaning: Using warships to stop ships from entering or leaving a port or area.
A narrow sea route between Iran and Oman used for a large share of the world's oil.
A conflict becoming more serious or widening.

levels.headline: Hormuz attacks continue as US and Iran remain at a stalemate
levels.body:
Two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz this week, and Iranian officials told Reuters they are deploying new tactics against ships using the waterway. The war involving Iran began on 28 February, and the strait remains the central flashpoint.
The United States maintains a blockade on Iranian oil. A US State Department spokesperson said oil shipments through the strait have passed pre-conflict levels, excluding Iranian oil, but a live tracker still describes the strait as effectively closed to commercial shipping. The two accounts cannot both be fully right, and the picture is hard to confirm independently.
On 8 October Euronews reported that President Donald Trump was weighing whether to resume major combat operations in Iran. Efforts to end the war have stalled. The IMF's growth forecast this week assumes that shipments through Hormuz resume by March.
levels.why: The strait carries a large share of the world's oil, so the conflict affects prices and growth everywhere.

levels.headline: US and Iran locked in a stand-off as ships are hit near Hormuz
levels.body:
Two vessels were hit in the Strait of Hormuz this week, and Iranian officials have told Reuters they are using new tactics against ships. The war, which began on 28 February, shows no sign of ending and the strait is its main flashpoint.
Washington keeps up a blockade of Iranian oil. A State Department spokesperson says other oil shipments through the strait have exceeded pre-war levels, but a live tracker says the route is effectively closed to commercial traffic. The conflicting claims are hard to check independently.
Euronews reported on 8 October that President Trump was considering resuming major combat operations. Peace efforts have stalled. The IMF's new forecast assumes that shipping through Hormuz restarts by March, which depends on the standoff easing.
levels.why: The outcome will decide oil prices, inflation and growth well beyond the Middle East.

levels.headline: Ships struck near Hormuz as there is no end in sight to the Iran war
levels.body:
Two ships were struck in the Strait of Hormuz this week. Iranian officials told Reuters that they are using new tactics to attack vessels there. The war involving Iran started on 28 February, and the strait is where much of the fighting is focused.
The United States is blocking Iranian oil. A State Department spokesperson said that other oil is moving through the strait at higher levels than before the conflict. A live tracking website, though, says the strait is effectively closed to commercial ships. It is hard to confirm which is right.
On 8 October, Euronews reported that President Trump was considering restarting major combat operations. Talks to end the war have stalled. The IMF assumes ships will be able to use the strait again by March.
levels.why: A lot of the world's oil moves through the strait, so the fighting affects prices everywhere.

levels.headline: The Iran war goes on, and ships are being hit near a key sea route
levels.body:
A war involving Iran has been going on since 28 February. This week two ships were hit in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route. Iran told the news agency Reuters that it is using new ways to attack ships.
The United States is stopping Iranian oil from leaving, which is called a blockade. A US official says other oil is passing through the strait at higher levels than before the war. But a tracking website says the strait is almost closed to ordinary ships. It is hard to know which is correct.
On 8 October, a news report said President Trump was thinking about starting major attacks again. Talks to end the war have not got anywhere. The IMF, a group that studies the world economy, hopes ships can use the strait again by March.
levels.why: A lot of the world's oil goes through the strait, so the war affects prices everywhere.

levels.headline: The Iran war goes on, with ships hit near a key sea route
levels.body:
A war involving Iran began on 28 February, and much of it centres on the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route used by many oil ships. This week two vessels were struck, and Iranian officials told Reuters they are using new tactics.
The United States is blockading Iranian oil. A State Department spokesperson says other oil is passing through the strait at higher levels than before the war, but a tracking website says it is effectively closed to commercial ships. It is hard to confirm which is right.
Euronews reported on 8 October that President Trump was weighing a return to major combat operations. Talks to end the war have stalled. The IMF's forecast assumes shipping through the strait resumes by March.
levels.why: The strait carries a large share of the world's oil, so the war affects prices everywhere.

levels.headline: Fighting near an important sea route has no end in sight
levels.body:
There is a war involving Iran that began on 28 February. Much of the fighting is around the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow stretch of sea that many oil ships use. This week two ships were hit. Iran says it has new ways to attack them.
The United States is stopping Iranian oil from leaving the area. This is called a blockade. A US official says that other ships are carrying more oil than before the war. But a website that tracks ships says the strait is almost shut. It is hard to know who is right.
A news report said the US president, Donald Trump, was thinking of starting big attacks again. Talks to end the war have stopped. People hope ships can use the strait safely by March.
levels.why: The war affects fuel prices around the world.

levels.headline: A war near a key sea route is not ending
levels.body:
A country called Iran is in a war. It started on 28 February. A lot of the fighting is happening around a narrow sea path called the Strait of Hormuz. Many ships carrying oil use this path. This week, two ships were hit. Iran said it has new ways to attack them.
The United States is trying to stop Iranian oil from leaving. It says other oil ships are getting through. But a website that watches ships says the path is almost closed. We cannot be sure who is right.
The American president, Donald Trump, was thinking about starting big attacks again, one report said. People who are trying to end the war have not agreed anything yet. Many people hope ships will be able to use the path safely by March.
levels.why: The war can make fuel more expensive for everyone.

levels.headline: A faraway war is making ships unsafe
levels.body:
There is a war far away in the Middle East. It involves a country called Iran. Ships that carry oil have to sail through a narrow sea path called the Strait of Hormuz. This week two of the ships were hit.
The United States says oil ships are still getting through. But another website says the path is almost closed. It is hard to know who is right.
The American president, Donald Trump, is thinking about what to do next. People trying to end the war have not yet made a deal. Many grown-ups hope that the sea path will be safe again soon. When it is not safe, oil becomes dearer, and that makes fuel cost more.
levels.why: The war can make fuel cost more for everyone.

levels.headline: Ships are in danger far away, and it matters here
levels.body:
A long way away, there is a war. Ships carry oil along a narrow sea path there. Some ships were hit this week. That is scary for the sailors, and it makes ship owners nervous.
Grown-ups in charge of countries are trying to decide what to do. They have not been able to agree how to stop the fighting. Some say lots of ships are getting through. Others say the path is almost shut. It is hard to be sure.
It matters to us because oil is used to make fuel. If the ships cannot get through, fuel can cost more. Then lorries, cars and shops all have to pay more. Everybody hopes the fighting will stop soon.
levels.why: It matters because the war can make fuel cost more.

levels.headline: Why a war far away can change prices here
levels.body:
Imagine a narrow corridor at school that everyone has to use to get to the dinner hall. If the corridor gets blocked, lunch is late. There is a corridor like that at sea. Ships that carry oil have to sail through it. This week some ships were hit there, because of a war.
People in charge of countries are trying to find a way to stop it, but they have not yet. Some say plenty of ships are getting through. Others say the corridor is almost closed. It is hard to know.
Oil is used to make fuel. So if the ships are blocked, fuel costs more. Everyone hopes the fighting stops.
levels.why: It matters because the war can make fuel cost more.

headline: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, but there is no Kremlin confirmation

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a time.
Penalties, usually economic, imposed on a country to pressure it to change its behaviour.
Power plants, refineries, pipelines and other sites that supply fuel and electricity.

levels.headline: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, but there is no Kremlin confirmation
levels.body:
President Donald Trump said on Sunday 11 October that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, meaning both sides would stop attacking each other's energy facilities. Neither side has clearly confirmed it, and there has been no official Kremlin confirmation or detail on its terms or start date.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will agree if Russia does, and asked Mr Trump to say when it begins. Ukraine has offered to stop hitting refineries if Russia halts its attacks on Ukrainian energy sites. Russia struck Ukrainian energy sites overnight, and at least 20 people died in strikes on residential buildings on Saturday, hours after the latest talks in the United States were cut short by a day.
The announcement came amid a dispute over a US deal easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's office said the agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and their allies, and seven US senators said it breaches the 2022 ban on Russian energy imports.
levels.why: A real halt to energy strikes would ease pressure on Ukrainian civilians and could affect energy prices.

levels.headline: Energy ceasefire claimed by Trump, but Russia has not confirmed it
levels.body:
On Sunday 11 October, President Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy facilities with immediate effect. Neither government has clearly confirmed this, and the Kremlin has not publicly backed it. No terms or start date have been given. Mr Trump made a similar claim last month, and the war continued.
President Zelensky said Ukraine would agree if Russia did and asked when it would start. Kyiv has offered to stop hitting Russian refineries if Moscow stops attacking its energy sites. Russia hit Ukrainian energy sites overnight, and at least 20 people were killed in attacks on homes on Saturday, soon after talks in the US ended a day early.
The claim follows controversy over a US deal easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney opposed it, and seven US senators said it broke the ban on Russian energy imports that Congress passed in 2022.
levels.why: It matters for Ukrainian civilians, for European energy supplies and for oil and diesel prices.

levels.headline: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree energy truce, but the details are unclear
levels.body:
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an energy ceasefire, which would stop attacks on each other's energy sites starting immediately. Neither side has clearly confirmed it. The Kremlin has not said anything official, and no start date has been given. Mr Trump made a similar claim last month, and fighting went on.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said his country will agree if Russia does. He asked Mr Trump to say when it begins. Ukraine says it will stop hitting refineries if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy sites. Russia attacked Ukrainian energy sites overnight. At least 20 people died in strikes on homes on Saturday.
The announcement came amid a row over a US deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, opposed it, and seven US senators said it was illegal.
levels.why: It could ease the war's effect on civilians and on energy prices, if it is real.

levels.headline: A truce on energy attacks is announced, but nobody has confirmed it
levels.body:
The American president, Donald Trump, said on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop attacking each other's energy sites. This would mean power stations and oil refineries. He said it would start immediately. But neither country has clearly agreed. The Russian government has not said it officially, and there is no start date.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said Ukraine would agree if Russia does. He wants to know when it starts. Russia attacked Ukrainian energy sites overnight. At least 20 people died on Saturday when homes were hit.
There is also an argument about sanctions. Sanctions are penalties on a country. The US made a deal that eased sanctions on Russian diesel. Canada's prime minister said this goes against what Ukraine and its friends are trying to do. Seven US senators said it was against the law.
levels.why: It matters for people in Ukraine and for the price of fuel.

levels.headline: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agreed an energy truce, but it is unconfirmed
levels.body:
On Sunday 11 October, President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy sites, such as power stations and refineries. A ceasefire is an agreement to stop fighting. Neither country has clearly confirmed it, the Kremlin has said nothing official, and no start date has been given.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would agree if Russia does. Russia struck Ukrainian energy sites overnight, and at least 20 people died when homes were hit on Saturday.
There is also a row over a US deal that eased sanctions on Russian diesel. Sanctions are penalties meant to pressure a country. Canada's prime minister opposed the deal, and seven US senators said it was illegal.
levels.why: If real, it could make life safer in Ukraine and ease fuel prices.

levels.headline: Is there a deal to stop attacks on power stations? Not yet confirmed
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine are at war. Both have been attacking the other's energy sites, like power stations and oil refineries. On Sunday, the American president, Donald Trump, said both sides had agreed to stop. But the two countries have not clearly said so. Russia has said nothing official, and nobody knows the start date.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said Ukraine would stop if Russia did. Russia hit Ukrainian energy sites overnight. At least 20 people died on Saturday when homes were hit by attacks.
There is also an argument about a US deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. Sanctions are penalties that are meant to put pressure on a country. Canada's prime minister and seven US senators have said they do not agree with the deal.
levels.why: If it is real, it could make life safer for people in Ukraine and lower fuel prices.

levels.headline: A promise to stop attacking power stations, but is it real?
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine are fighting a war. Each country has been attacking the other's power stations and fuel sites. On Sunday the American president, Donald Trump, said both countries had agreed to stop. But neither has clearly said yes. Russia has not said anything official.
The president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, says Ukraine will stop if Russia does. On Saturday, at least 20 people were killed when homes were hit. Russia also attacked energy sites overnight. So the fighting has not stopped.
There is also an argument about fuel. The United States made a deal that lets Russia sell more diesel. Some other countries and American senators do not like this. They say it helps Russia, and one group says it is against the law.
levels.why: If it works, people in Ukraine would be safer.

levels.headline: Two countries may stop a type of fighting, but nobody is sure
levels.body:
Two countries, Russia and Ukraine, are fighting a war. Each one has been hitting the other's power stations and fuel sites. On Sunday the American president, Donald Trump, said they had both agreed to stop. But the countries themselves have not said yes clearly.
The leader of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, says Ukraine will stop if Russia does. But people are still being hurt. At least 20 people died on Saturday when homes were hit.
Some grown-ups are also cross about a deal on fuel that the US made with Russia. They say it is wrong. For now, nobody can say if the plan will work.
levels.why: If it works, people in Ukraine would be safer.

levels.headline: A promise to stop one kind of fighting
levels.body:
Two countries are fighting. They are called Russia and Ukraine. Sometimes they break each other's power stations, and then people have no lights or heat. On Sunday, a leader from America said both countries had agreed to stop doing that.
But the two countries have not both said yes. The leader of Ukraine said they will stop if Russia does. It is like when two children promise to stop a fight, but only if the other child does it first.
People are still being hurt. Grown-ups are watching to see if the promise will work.
levels.why: If it works, fewer people would lose power and be hurt.

levels.headline: Two sides promise to stop one kind of fighting
levels.body:
Two countries are in a long fight. They are called Russia and Ukraine. They have been breaking each other's power stations, so lights and heating stop working. A leader from America said on Sunday that both sides had said yes to stopping.
But it is not certain yet. Ukraine said it would stop if Russia did. It is like two friends who both say, you first. Nobody has been sure about it so far.
People are still being hurt, so lots of grown-ups hope the promise will be real. Then families could stay warm and safe.
levels.why: If it works, fewer people would lose power and be hurt.

headline: US sanctions the International Criminal Court hours after Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize

terms.meaning: The International Criminal Court in The Hague, which tries individuals accused of war crimes and genocide.
Penalties, usually economic, imposed to pressure a person, group or country.
A permit allowing some activity that sanctions would otherwise ban.

levels.headline: US sanctions the International Criminal Court hours after Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
levels.body:
The United States imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution on Friday 9 October, hours after the South African jurist Navi Pillay was named the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner. The measures block any assets the court may hold in US jurisdictions and give US companies and individuals doing business with it six months to wind that business down.
Earlier sanctions had targeted individual ICC judges and prosecutors. The US Treasury also issued four general licences allowing some activity, including payments linked to ICC telecommunications, software and pensions, and transactions linked to detainees. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US is not subject to the jurisdiction of what he called the fake ICC, adding that either the court ends its threats or the US will end the ICC.
Ms Pillay called the sanctions unacceptable. ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said they would not stop the court's work. One report notes the move was in preparation before the prize was announced.
levels.why: It tests whether international courts can work when a powerful state tries to shut them down.

levels.headline: US hits the ICC with sweeping sanctions on the day a Nobel Peace Prize goes to Navi Pillay
levels.body:
On Friday 9 October the United States sanctioned the International Criminal Court itself, hours after Navi Pillay of South Africa won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The sanctions freeze any court assets in US jurisdictions and give US firms and individuals six months to end their business with the court.
Previous sanctions had focused on individual judges and prosecutors. This time the Treasury also issued four general licences allowing limited activity, such as ICC telecommunications, software and pension payments. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US is not subject to the jurisdiction of the court, and that the ICC will either end its threats or the US will end the ICC.
Ms Pillay called the move unacceptable, and the ICC's deputy prosecutor said its work would continue. The Nobel committee chair said international law is under tremendous pressure. One report says the sanctions had been planned before the prize.
levels.why: It raises the question of whether a major power can effectively shut down an international court.

levels.headline: The US imposes sanctions on the International Criminal Court after Nobel announcement
levels.body:
The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court, the court in The Hague that tries people accused of the gravest crimes. The announcement on Friday 9 October came hours after Navi Pillay of South Africa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Under the sanctions, any assets the court holds in US jurisdictions are blocked, and US businesses and people working with it have six months to stop.
The US had already sanctioned some ICC judges and prosecutors. Now the whole institution is covered, though four general licences allow some payments, such as for telecoms, software and pensions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the ICC would either end its threats or the US would end the court.
Ms Pillay said the sanctions were unacceptable. The ICC's deputy prosecutor said its work would not stop. Some reports say the sanctions had been planned for some time.
levels.why: It affects whether an international court can keep working under pressure from a major power.

levels.headline: The US punishes the International Criminal Court with sanctions
levels.body:
The International Criminal Court, or ICC, is a court in The Hague. It tries people accused of terrible crimes like war crimes. On Friday 9 October, the United States put sanctions on the court itself. Sanctions are penalties. The US will block any money the court has in the US. American firms and people who work with the court have six months to stop.
The news came hours after Navi Pillay, a legal expert from South Africa, won the Nobel Peace Prize. The US had already put sanctions on some of the court's judges and prosecutors. Now it covers the whole court, though some payments are still allowed.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the ICC must stop its threats, or the US will end it. Ms Pillay said the sanctions are unacceptable. The court says it will keep working.
levels.why: It could limit whether the court can keep doing its job.

levels.headline: The US puts sanctions on the International Criminal Court
levels.body:
The International Criminal Court, or ICC, is a court in The Hague that tries people accused of the gravest crimes, such as war crimes. On Friday 9 October, the United States put sanctions on the whole court. Sanctions are penalties. Any assets the court holds in US jurisdictions are blocked, and US companies and people working with it have six months to stop.
This came hours after Navi Pillay of South Africa won the Nobel Peace Prize. The US had already sanctioned individual ICC judges and prosecutors. Four general licences still allow some payments, such as for telecoms, software and pensions.

levels.why: It tests whether an international court can keep working under pressure.

levels.headline: The US puts penalties on a world court
levels.body:
The ICC is a court in a city called The Hague. It tries people accused of very bad crimes, like crimes in wars. The United States does not agree with it. On Friday 9 October, the US put penalties, called sanctions, on the whole court. This means that any money the court has in the US is blocked. American companies have six months to stop working with it.
This happened hours after a woman called Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize. She is a legal expert from South Africa. The US had already put penalties on some of the court's judges.
The US official, Marco Rubio, said that the court must stop, or the US will end it. Ms Pillay said the penalties are not acceptable. The court says that it will keep going.
levels.why: It tests whether an international court can keep working under pressure.

levels.headline: America puts penalties on a world court, just after a big prize
levels.body:
There is a court in a city called The Hague. It is called the International Criminal Court. It tries people who are accused of very serious crimes. The United States is not happy with it. On Friday 9 October, it put penalties on the whole court. These are called sanctions. Any money the court has in America is blocked.
This was just after a legal expert called Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize. This is a famous prize for people who work for peace. She said the penalties on the court are not acceptable.
An American leader, Marco Rubio, said the court must stop its threats, or the US will end it. The court says it will carry on with its work.
levels.why: It tests whether a world court can keep working.

levels.headline: A big country punishes a world court
levels.body:
Some crimes are so serious that they are looked at by a special court for the whole world. It is called the International Criminal Court. America does not like it. On Friday, America put penalties on it. This means American companies must stop working with it.
The same day, a woman called Navi Pillay won a famous prize for peace. She said that the penalties were wrong.
An American leader said the court must stop what it is doing, or America will end it. The court said it would carry on. Many people are watching to see what happens next.
levels.why: It tests whether a world court can keep working.

levels.headline: A big country and a court for the whole world
levels.body:
There is a court for the whole world that looks at very serious crimes. America is not happy with it. This week America punished the court. It said American companies must stop working with it.
This was on the same day that a lady called Navi Pillay won a big prize for peace. She said the punishment was wrong.
It is a bit like a big boy telling the referee that he doesn't like the rules and making things hard for him. The court said it will carry on with its job. Lots of grown-ups are watching.
levels.why: It tests whether the world court can keep working.

levels.headline: A court that wants everyone to follow the rules
levels.body:
Imagine a game where one referee has to be fair to everyone. There is a referee like that for the whole world. It is called a court. It looks at very serious bad things that people do.
This week, a big country punished the court because it did not like it. The big country said the court must stop, or it would end it. The court said no. It will keep doing its job.
On the same day, a lady who had been a judge won a famous prize for peace. She said the punishment was wrong. Many people are watching what happens next.
levels.why: It tests whether the world court can keep working.
